source_refs.note: Chapter 20 exercise (PDF 166-168, printed 162-164), solved: 9 MCQs with keys worked out from the chapter (the book prints no key), model answers to 8 short, 6 constructed and 6 comprehensive questions, and 4 numericals worked step by step.

blocks.prompt: 20.1 What kind of radiation is detected in a PET scan after positron annihilation?
blocks.explanation: The positron from the tracer meets an electron and both annihilate; their mass is converted into two gamma-ray photons moving in opposite directions, which the ring of detectors records.

blocks.prompt: 20.2 What is the role of coincidence detection in PET-scanning?

options.text: To control the temperature of the scanner
To detect gamma rays arriving simultaneously

blocks.explanation: The two gamma photons of one annihilation travel in opposite directions and reach opposite detectors at (almost) the same time. Detecting them in coincidence shows that they came from one event on the line joining the two detectors, so the event can be located.

blocks.prompt: 20.3 Which principle allows ultrasound transducers to emit and detect sound waves?
blocks.explanation: An alternating voltage makes the piezoelectric crystal vibrate and send out ultrasound (converse piezoelectric effect); the returning echoes squeeze the crystal and produce a voltage (direct piezoelectric effect).

blocks.prompt: 20.4 Which body part is commonly examined using ultrasound imaging?
blocks.explanation: Ultrasound images soft tissues well. In the abdominal region it examines the liver, kidneys, gallbladder, pancreas and bladder. Bone reflects almost all the ultrasound, so skull, bones and teeth are not imaged this way.

blocks.prompt: 20.5 In X-ray imaging, what does "contrast" mainly depend on?
blocks.explanation: Contrast is the difference in brightness between tissues. It comes from their different absorption (attenuation) of X-rays, I = I₀e^(−μx), which depends on the density (and atomic number) of the tissue and its thickness x (and on the X-ray energy).

blocks.prompt: 20.6 What advantage does a CT scan have over a standard X-ray image?

options.text: Uses sound waves instead of X-rays

blocks.explanation: A CT scanner takes X-ray images of a body section from many angles; the computer makes cross-sectional (2D) slices and combines them into a 3D image. CT gives a larger dose, needs more complex equipment and still uses X-rays.

blocks.prompt: 20.7 What kind of wave is used in ultrasound imaging?
blocks.explanation: Ultrasound is a high-frequency sound wave (1 MHz-15 MHz). Sound travels through tissues as a longitudinal (compression) wave; it is a mechanical wave, not electromagnetic, and it is non-ionizing.

blocks.prompt: 20.8 Characteristic X-rays are produced due to:
blocks.explanation: A fast electron knocks out an inner (K or L) shell electron of a heavy target atom; an electron from a higher shell fills the hole and emits an X-ray photon, e.g. hf(Kα) = E_L − E_K. Their energies depend on the target material, hence 'characteristic'.

blocks.prompt: 20.9 What does CT stand for in medical imaging?
blocks.explanation: CT = Computed Tomography: 'computed' because a computer processes the data, 'tomography' from the Greek tomos, meaning slice.

blocks.prompt: 20.1 Which type of radiation is produced during a PET scan?
blocks.explanation: Gamma rays. The tracer emits positrons; each positron annihilates with an electron of the tissue and their mass is converted into two gamma-ray photons that move in opposite directions. These gamma rays are detected by the detector ring.

blocks.prompt: 20.2 Which physical effect enables ultrasound transducers to produce sound waves?
blocks.explanation: The piezoelectric effect (its converse form). An alternating voltage applied to the piezoelectric crystal (e.g. quartz, PZT) makes it expand and contract rapidly, so it vibrates and sends out ultrasound waves. Returning echoes produce a voltage across it (direct effect).

blocks.prompt: 20.3 Mention one area of the body commonly examined using ultrasound.
blocks.explanation: The abdomen (liver, kidneys, gallbladder, pancreas and bladder). Ultrasound is also used to monitor the fetus during pregnancy and to study the heart (echocardiography).

blocks.prompt: 20.4 What causes contrast in X-ray images of different body tissues?
blocks.explanation: Different tissues absorb (attenuate) X-rays by different amounts, I = I₀e^(−μx); μ depends on the density and atomic number of the tissue and on the X-ray energy. Bone absorbs more and looks white; soft tissue and air absorb less and look grey or dark.

blocks.prompt: 20.5 State one major difference between a CT scan and a standard X-ray image.
blocks.explanation: A standard X-ray gives a flat 2D image in which bones and organs overlap, while a CT scan gives cross-sectional slices combined into a 3D image, so each structure is seen separately at its exact position.

rows: Cross-sectional slices and a 3D image
A single flat 2D image
No overlapping of organs
Front and back structures overlap

blocks.prompt: 20.6 What occurs when ultrasound hits the boundary between two tissues?
blocks.explanation: Part of the wave is reflected back as an echo and the rest is transmitted into the next tissue. The larger the difference in acoustic impedance of the two tissues, the stronger the echo; the transducer detects the echo to build the image.

blocks.prompt: 20.7 What does the abbreviation "CT" stand for, and how does it improve imaging?
blocks.explanation: CT stands for Computed Tomography. The X-ray tube rotates around the patient and takes images from many angles; a computer makes cross-sectional slices and combines them into a 3D image. This removes overlapping and shows the size, shape and exact location of organs and tumours, even of tissues with similar densities.

blocks.prompt: 20.8 What do you know about the terms kα, kβ, kₚ, X-rays.
blocks.explanation: They are characteristic X-rays emitted when a vacancy in the K-shell of a heavy target atom is filled. Kα: an electron jumps from the L-shell to the K-shell, hf = E_L − E_K. Kβ: from the M-shell to the K-shell, hf = E_M − E_K (more energetic than Kα). The next line, from the N-shell to the K-shell (hf = E_N − E_K), is Kγ. Their energies depend on the target material.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question prints the terms as "kα, kβ, kₚ". These are the K-series lines Kα, Kβ and Kγ (capital K for the K-shell); the third term "kₚ" should read Kγ.

blocks.prompt: 20.1 What does a time difference in detecting gamma rays at two detectors indicate in a PET scan?
blocks.explanation:
The two gamma photons from one annihilation leave in opposite directions at the same speed c.
1. If they reach the two opposite detectors at the same time, the annihilation took place at the midpoint of the line joining the detectors.
2. A small time difference Δt shows that the event was nearer to the detector that fired first; its distance from the midpoint is d = cΔt/2. This (time-of-flight) information locates the tracer along the line and sharpens the image.
3. If the time difference is larger than the short coincidence window (a few nanoseconds), the two photons are not from the same annihilation and the pair is rejected.

blocks.prompt: 20.2 Why is ultrasound not effective for imaging air-filled organs like the lungs?
blocks.explanation:
1. Echoes form at boundaries of different acoustic impedance. The impedance of air is extremely small compared with soft tissue, so at a tissue-air boundary almost all the ultrasound is reflected back and hardly any enters the lung.
2. The little that enters is strongly absorbed and scattered by the air in the lungs.
3. So no useful echoes come from inside the lung; only a bright line at its surface is seen. (For the same reason gel is used to remove air between the probe and the skin.) Lungs are imaged with X-rays or CT.

blocks.prompt: 20.3 What happens when the X-ray contrast between two tissues is too low? Suggest a solution.
blocks.explanation:
When the two tissues absorb X-rays almost equally (similar density, atomic number and thickness), they appear in nearly the same shade of grey. Their boundary cannot be seen and a disease or injury may be missed.
Solutions:
1. Use a contrast medium of high atomic number, such as iodine (Z = 53, injected) or barium (Z = 56, swallowed as a barium meal). It absorbs X-rays strongly and makes that organ stand out.
2. Choose a suitable X-ray energy: soft (low-energy) X-rays for soft tissues such as the breast, hard X-rays for bone.
3. Use a CT scan, which can distinguish tissues of very similar densities.

blocks.prompt: 20.4 How does CT scanning reduce the overlapping of organs seen in plain X-rays?
blocks.explanation:
1. In a plain X-ray all the structures along the path of the beam are recorded on one flat 2D image, so they overlap (e.g. the front and back ribs).
2. In CT, the X-ray tube rotates around the patient and sends the beam through one thin slice of the body from many angles; detectors on the opposite side record each view.
3. The computer combines these views to build a cross-sectional image of that slice only, so organs above or below it do not overlap it.
4. The couch moves a little and the next slice is taken; the slices are combined into a 3D image, in which each organ is seen at its own position.

blocks.prompt: 20.5 What could be a possible medical cause of uneven tracer concentration seen in a PET brain scan?
blocks.explanation:
The tracer collects more in tissues that are very active (use more glucose) and less in inactive ones, so uneven concentration shows abnormal activity:
1. Bright "hot spots" (high uptake): a brain tumour, because cancer cells are very active and use much more glucose; or the focus of an epileptic seizure during the seizure.
2. Dark "cold spots" (low uptake): regions with little activity or blood supply, e.g. after a stroke, or in dementia such as Alzheimer's disease.
(Normal brain activity also varies a little from region to region.)

blocks.prompt: 20.6 What is the purpose of lead collimators in PET gamma-ray detectors?
20.1 What is the piezoelectric effect, and how does it allow transducers to both emit and detect ultrasound waves?
blocks.explanation:
Piezoelectric effect:
1. The word comes from the Greek "piezein", to press. The effect was discovered in 1880 by Pierre Curie and Jacques Curie with crystals such as quartz, tourmaline and Rochelle salt; PZT (lead zirconate titanate) is used in probes today.
2. These crystals have no centre of symmetry. Inside them, positive and negative charges are normally balanced.
3. Direct piezoelectric effect: when mechanical pressure is applied, the charges shift slightly, the balance is disturbed and an electric charge (voltage) appears on the surfaces. Pressure is turned into voltage.
4. Converse piezoelectric effect: when an electric field (voltage) is applied to the crystal, it changes shape slightly. Voltage is turned into mechanical movement.
The transducer as emitter and detector:
1. Emitting: an alternating voltage of ultrasonic frequency (1 MHz-15 MHz) is applied to the crystal. By the converse effect it expands and contracts at the same frequency, vibrates, and sends a short pulse of ultrasound into the body through the gel.
2. Detecting: the transducer then switches to receive mode. The echoes reflected from tissue boundaries strike the crystal and squeeze it; by the direct effect it produces small voltages.
3. These electrical signals go to the computer, which uses their time delay and strength to make the image.
So the same crystal turns electrical energy into sound and sound back into electrical signals; this dual role makes one probe both the emitter and the detector.

blocks.prompt: 20.2 Describe how an ultrasound image is created using the concepts of echoes and reflected sound waves.
blocks.explanation:
Ultrasound imaging works on the pulse-echo principle:
1. Gel is applied between the transducer and the skin to remove air gaps, so that the sound enters the body.
2. The piezoelectric transducer sends short pulses of high-frequency sound (1 MHz-15 MHz) into the body. The waves travel through tissues at speeds that depend on the type of tissue.
3. At each boundary between two tissues of different acoustic impedance (which depends on the tissue density and the speed of sound in it), part of the wave is reflected as an echo; the rest goes deeper and is reflected at deeper boundaries.
4. The transducer switches to receive mode and detects the echoes by the direct piezoelectric effect, turning them into electrical signals.
5. The computer measures the time delay t of each echo. The sound goes to the boundary and back, so its depth is d = vt/2 (v is about 1540 m s⁻¹ in soft tissue). For example, an echo returning after 100 µs comes from d = (1540 m s⁻¹ × 100 × 10⁻⁶ s)/2 ≈ 7.7 cm.
6. The intensity of each echo sets the brightness: stronger reflections (larger impedance difference, e.g. tissue-bone) appear brighter.
7. By sweeping the beam along many lines, the computer builds a 2D image of the organs in real time.
Image quality: a larger impedance difference gives clearer boundaries; higher frequency gives better resolution but less penetration; the gel improves transmission. Example: echoes from the boundaries between the amniotic fluid and the fetus show the baby in pregnancy.

blocks.prompt: 20.3 Explain how the absorption (attenuation) of X-rays by different tissues creates contrast in the resulting image. Include an example.
blocks.explanation:
Attenuation:
1. As X-rays pass through the body they interact with atoms (they can ionize them), lose energy and are partly absorbed or scattered. This is attenuation.
2. The intensity falls exponentially with thickness: I = I₀e^(−μx), where I₀ is the initial intensity, I the intensity after passing through thickness x, and μ the attenuation coefficient, which depends on the material (its density and atomic number) and on the X-ray energy.
Contrast:
1. Different tissues have different μ and thickness, so different amounts of X-rays get through them to the film or detector.
2. Bone (dense, contains calcium) has a large μ and absorbs most X-rays: little reaches the detector and bone looks white.
3. Soft tissues (muscle, fat, organs) absorb less and look grey; air in the lungs absorbs very little and looks dark.
4. This difference in transmitted intensity, which lets us tell tissues apart, is the contrast. Contrast also depends on the X-ray energy: hard X-rays are used for bones, soft X-rays for soft tissues such as the breast.
Example: in a chest X-ray the ribs and spine appear white, the heart grey and the air-filled lungs dark; a fracture shows as a dark line across a white bone, because X-rays pass through the gap. Where two soft tissues absorb almost equally, a contrast medium such as barium (Z = 56, barium meal for the stomach and intestine) or iodine (Z = 53, for blood vessels) is used to increase absorption and make them stand out.

blocks.prompt: 20.4 Compare CT and conventional X-ray imaging with respect to image clarity and diagnostic value.
blocks.explanation: A CT scan gives far clearer, more detailed images with much greater diagnostic value, at the cost of a higher radiation dose, time and expense; a conventional X-ray is quick and simple and is enough for many purposes such as fractures.

Clarity: a single flat 2D image
Organs do not overlap; each is seen at its own position
Organs overlap (e.g. front and back ribs)
Distinguishes tissues of very similar densities
Poor contrast between soft tissues of similar density
Shows the size, shape and exact location of organs and tumours
Shows only the outline of structures in one view
Diagnostic value: tumours, internal injuries and bleeding, strokes within minutes; guides treatment (e.g. aiming radiation at a tumour)
Diagnostic value: mainly bones (fractures), chest and teeth; useful, quick first check

blocks.prompt: 20.5 Define tomography and explain how CT scanning creates 3D images using 2D slices.
blocks.explanation:
Tomography: imaging the body section by section, i.e. forming an image of one thin slice (cross-section) of the body. The word comes from the Greek "tomos", meaning slice.
How CT makes 3D images (Computed Axial Tomography):
1. The patient lies on a couch inside a ring of X-ray detectors; the X-ray tube is on the ring opposite the activated detectors.
2. The X-ray tube rotates around the patient and sends a thin beam through one slice of the body from many different angles. For each angle the detectors on the opposite side measure how much the beam has been attenuated.
3. A computer combines these many views and calculates how much each small part of the slice absorbs. From this it builds a detailed 2D cross-sectional image of that slice, with no overlapping of structures.
4. The couch then moves the patient slightly along the axis of the body and the process is repeated for the next slice. Hundreds of slices are taken in seconds.
5. The computer stacks all these 2D slices, like the layers of a cake, to form a 3D image of the internal structure, which shows the size, shape and exact position of organs, bones and tumours.
(The CT scanner was invented by Godfrey Hounsfield and Allan Cormack in the early 1970s; Nobel Prize 1979.)

blocks.prompt: 20.6 How would you explain the inner shell transitions of X-rays? Also explain characteristic and continues X-rays.
blocks.explanation:
Inner shell transitions:
1. In heavy atoms the electrons are arranged in shells K, L, M, N, ..., the K-shell being closest to the nucleus. Inner-shell electrons are tightly bound, so the energy differences between inner shells are large.
2. In an X-ray tube, electrons from the heated cathode are accelerated through a potential difference V and strike a heavy target (e.g. tungsten) with (K.E.)ₘₐₓ = Ve.
3. A fast electron may knock out an electron from the K-shell, leaving a vacancy (hole).
4. An electron from the L-shell jumps into the hole and emits a photon hf(Kα) = E_L − E_K (Kα X-ray). If an electron from the M-shell fills it, hf(Kβ) = E_M − E_K (Kβ X-ray), and so on. The holes left in the L and M shells are filled from higher shells, giving more X-rays.
5. Because these energy differences are large, the photons are X-rays.
Characteristic X-rays: the photons emitted in these inner-shell transitions. They have definite wavelengths that depend on the target material, and appear as sharp lines (peaks) on the continuous spectrum. Their study has helped in understanding atomic structure and the periodic table.
Continuous X-rays (bremsstrahlung, braking radiation): when the fast electrons hit the target they are suddenly decelerated. An accelerating (decelerating) charge emits electromagnetic radiation; the deceleration is very large, so the radiation is in the X-ray region. An electron that loses all its kinetic energy in one collision gives the most energetic photon: Ve = hfₘₐₓ = hc/λₘᵢₙ. Other electrons lose energy in several collisions and give photons of lower energy (longer wavelength), so a continuous range of wavelengths above λₘᵢₙ is produced. The characteristic lines appear on this continuous spectrum (Fig. 20.6).

rows: Produced by inner-shell electron transitions (e.g. L → K)
Produced by the sudden deceleration of fast electrons (bremsstrahlung)
Definite wavelengths: sharp lines
All wavelengths above λₘᵢₙ: a continuous spectrum
Wavelengths depend on the target material
λₘᵢₙ = hc/(Ve) depends on the accelerating voltage, not on the target

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question prints "continues X-rays"; it means "continuous X-rays".

blocks.prompt: 20.1 An electron jumps from a level Eᵢ = −3.5 × 10⁻¹⁹ J to E_f = −1.20 × 10⁻¹⁸ J. What is the wavelength of the emitted light? (Ans: 234 nm)
blocks.explanation:
Given: Eᵢ = −3.5 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, E_f = −1.20 × 10⁻¹⁸ J = −12.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹
Required: λ
Energy of the emitted photon: hf = Eᵢ − E_f
ΔE = −3.5 × 10⁻¹⁹ J − (−12.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)
ΔE = 8.5 × 10⁻¹⁹ J
hc/λ = ΔE, so λ = hc/ΔE
λ = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s × 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)/(8.5 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)
λ = (1.989 × 10⁻²⁵ J m)/(8.5 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)
λ = 2.34 × 10⁻⁷ m = 234 nm
Answer: λ = 234 nm (agrees with the book).

blocks.prompt: 20.2 Electrons in an X-ray tube are accelerated through a potential difference of 3000 V. If these electrons were slowed down in a target, what will be the minimum wavelength of X-rays produced? (Ans: 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁰ m)
blocks.explanation:
Given: V = 3000 V, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹
Required: λₘᵢₙ
The shortest wavelength is produced when an electron loses all its kinetic energy in one collision:
(K.E.)ₘₐₓ = Ve = hfₘₐₓ = hc/λₘᵢₙ
λₘᵢₙ = hc/(Ve)
Ve = 3000 V × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C = 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁶ J
λₘᵢₙ = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s × 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)/(4.8 × 10⁻¹⁶ J)
λₘᵢₙ = (1.989 × 10⁻²⁵ J m)/(4.8 × 10⁻¹⁶ J)
λₘᵢₙ = 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁰ m
Answer: λₘᵢₙ = 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁰ m (agrees with the book).

blocks.prompt: 20.3 The wavelength of K X-ray from copper is 1.377 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. What is the energy difference between the two levels from which this transition results? (Ans: 9.03 KeV)
blocks.explanation:
Given: λ = 1.377 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J
Required: ΔE
The energy difference of the levels equals the photon energy:
ΔE = hf = hc/λ
ΔE = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s × 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)/(1.377 × 10⁻¹⁰ m)
ΔE = (1.989 × 10⁻²⁵ J m)/(1.377 × 10⁻¹⁰ m)
ΔE = 1.44 × 10⁻¹⁵ J
In electron volts: ΔE = (1.444 × 10⁻¹⁵ J)/(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J eV⁻¹) = 9.03 × 10³ eV
ΔE = 9.03 keV
Answer: ΔE = 1.44 × 10⁻¹⁵ J = 9.03 keV (agrees with the book).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed answer writes the unit as "KeV"; the correct symbol is keV (kilo-electron volt, small k). The value 9.03 keV is right.

blocks.prompt: 20.4 A tungsten target is struck by electrons that have been accelerated from rest through 40 kV potential difference. Find the shortest wavelength of the bremsstrahlung radiation emitted. (Ans: 0.31 × 10⁻¹⁰ m)
blocks.explanation:
Given: V = 40 kV = 4.0 × 10⁴ V, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹
Required: λₘᵢₙ
The shortest wavelength is emitted when an electron gives all its kinetic energy Ve to one photon:
Ve = hfₘₐₓ = hc/λₘᵢₙ
λₘᵢₙ = hc/(Ve)
Ve = 4.0 × 10⁴ V × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C = 6.4 × 10⁻¹⁵ J
λₘᵢₙ = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s × 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)/(6.4 × 10⁻¹⁵ J)
λₘᵢₙ = (1.989 × 10⁻²⁵ J m)/(6.4 × 10⁻¹⁵ J)
λₘᵢₙ = 3.1 × 10⁻¹¹ m = 0.31 × 10⁻¹⁰ m
Answer: λₘᵢₙ = 0.31 × 10⁻¹⁰ m (agrees with the book). It does not depend on the target being tungsten.
